title: XXIX. Papal claims on councils and Pope; three remaining questions
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss: From which we gather: about judicial interpretation properly so called (fitting law toward fact) there stands as no controversy, because both sides confess that councils plus that Pontiff can err in a question belonging toward fact; that controversy that remains stands as about didactic interpretation. But this stands as a claimed right — indeed pure ambition — that Hildebrandine claim thrust into that church some years ago. Bellarmine (On Councils 2.17) holds that that Pontiff stands as simply plus absolutely above that universal Church plus above a general council. (3) Is that Pope above a council? (2) Can that Pontiff err? Three questions remain: (1) Can a council err without the Pontiff or before his confirmation? On which councils plus how far they can err in interpretation, the papists disagree among themselves. For only the greater prelates — that stands as, bishops — ordinarily have decisive suffrage in councils; by privilege plus custom also cardinals plus general abbots belonging toward orders, even if not bishops; toward laity plus toward uncalled priests, none; toward those plus toward lesser clerics helping in debate they grant only consultative suffrage, as Bellarmine teaches. Further, judicial interpretation in the Papacy stands as ascribed partly toward a council, partly to the Roman Pontiff, partly to both together. XXIX.
pass_b_english: XXIX. Further, judicial interpretation in the Papacy is ascribed partly to a council, partly to the Roman Pontiff, partly to both together. For only the greater prelates — that is, bishops — ordinarily have decisive suffrage in councils; by privilege and custom also cardinals and general abbots of orders, even if not bishops; to laity and to uncalled priests, none; to those and to lesser clerics helping in debate they grant only consultative suffrage, as Bellarmine teaches. On which councils and how far they can err in interpretation, the papists disagree among themselves.

Three questions remain: (1) Can a council err without the Pontiff or before his confirmation? (2) Can the Pontiff err? (3) Is the Pope above a council? Bellarmine (On Councils 2.17) holds that the Pontiff is simply and absolutely above the universal Church and above a general council. But this is a claimed right — indeed pure ambition — the Hildebrandine claim thrust into the church some years ago. From which we gather: about judicial interpretation properly so called (fitting law to fact) there is no controversy, because both sides confess that councils and the Pontiff can err in a question of fact; the controversy that remains is about didactic interpretation.
source_text: XXIX. Porro interpretatio judicialis tum in Papatu partim concilio, partim Pontifici Romano, partim utrique simul tribuitur. Nam solos praelatos majores, eosque omnes, h.e. episcopos habere in conciliis jus suffragii decisivi ordinarie: ex privilegio autem & consuetudine etiam Cardinales, Abbates Generales ordinum, etiamsi non sint episcopi: laicis, quos vocant, & presbyteris, qui non vocantur, nullum: iis autem & clericis minoribus, viris doctis juvantibus in disputando, largiuntur duntaxat suffragium consultivum, ut docet Bellarminus. Quae vero concilia & quatenus errare possint in interpretatione, Pontificii inter se dissentiunt. Tres autem quaestiones supersunt: 1. An concilium, sine Pontifice vel ante confirmationem Pontificis errare possit? 2. An Pontifex errare possit? 3. An Papa sit supra concilium? Bellarminus lib.2. de concil. c.17. statuit, Pontificem simpliciter & absolute esse supra Ecclesiam universalem & supra concilium generale. Sed hoc est jus, imo pura puta ambitio, Hildebrandina in ecclesiam ab aliquot annis invecta. Ex quibus colligimus: de interpretatione judiciali proprie dicta, sive de accommodatione juris ad factum, nullam esse controversiam: quia fatentur utrinque, & concilia & Pontificem in quaestione facti errare posse: controversiam vero superesse de interpretatione didascalica.
